verses.zh: 申初祷告的时候，彼得、约翰上圣殿去。
verses.en: Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the time[NOTE:1] for prayer,[NOTE:2] at three o’clock in the afternoon.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “hour.”

Going up to the temple at the time for prayer. The earliest Christians, being of Jewish roots, were still participating in the institutions of Judaism at this point. Their faith in Christ did not make them non-Jewish in their practices.
Grk “at the ninth hour.” This is calculated from sunrise (Josephus, Ant. 14.4.3 [14.65]; Dan 9:21).

verses.zh: 有一个人，生来是瘸腿的，天天被人抬来，放在殿的一个门口（那门名叫美门），要求进殿的人周济。
verses.en: And a man lame[NOTE:1] from birth[NOTE:2] was being carried up, who was placed at the temple gate called “the Beautiful Gate” every day[NOTE:3] so he could beg for money[NOTE:4] from those going into the temple courts.[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “crippled.”
Grk “from his mother’s womb.”
BDAG 437 s.v. ἡμέρα 2.c has “every day” for this phrase.

Grk “alms.” The term “alms” is not in common use today, so what the man expected, “money,” is used in the translation instead. The idea is that of money given as a gift to someone who was poor. Giving alms was viewed as honorable in Judaism (Tob 1:3, 16; 12:8-9; m. Pe’ah 1:1). See also Luke 11:41; 12:33; Acts 9:36; 10:2, 4, 31; 24:17.

Grk “the temple.” This is actually a reference to the courts surrounding the temple proper, and has been translated accordingly.sn Into the temple courts. The exact location of this incident is debated. The ‘Beautiful Gate’ referred either to the Nicanor Gate (which led from the Court of the Gentiles into the Court of Women) or the Shushan Gate at the eastern wall.

verses.zh: 他看见彼得、约翰将要进殿，就求他们周济。
verses.en: When he saw Peter and John about to go into the temple courts,[NOTE:1] he asked them for money.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “the temple.” This is actually a reference to the courts surrounding the temple proper, and has been translated accordingly.sn See the note on the phrase the temple courts in the previous verse.
Grk “alms.” See the note on the word “money” in the previous verse.

verses.zh: 彼得、约翰定睛看他；彼得说：「你看我们！」
verses.en: Peter looked directly[NOTE:1] at him (as did John) and said, “Look at us!”
notes: Grk “Peter, looking directly at him, as did John, said.” The participle ἀτενίσας (atenisas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 那人就留意看他们，指望得着甚么。
verses.en: So the lame man[NOTE:1] paid attention to them, expecting to receive something from them.
notes: Grk “So he”; the referent (the lame man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 彼得说：「金银我都没有，只把我所有的给你：我奉拿撒勒人耶稣基督的名，叫你起来行走！」
verses.en: But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold,[NOTE:1] but what I do have I give you. In the name[NOTE:2] of Jesus Christ[NOTE:3] the Nazarene, stand up and[NOTE:4] walk!”
notes: Or “I have no money.” L&N 6.69 classifies the expression ἀργύριον καὶ χρυσίον (argurion kai chrusion) as an idiom that is a generic expression for currency, thus “money.”

In the name. Note the authority in the name of Jesus the Messiah. His presence and power are at work for the man. The reference to “the name” is not like a magical incantation, but is designed to indicate the agent who performs the healing. The theme is quite frequent in Acts (2:38 plus 21 other times).
Or “Messiah”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”

The words “stand up and” (ἔγειρε καί, egeire kai) are not in a few mss (א B D sa), but are included in A C E Ψ 095 33 1739 M lat sy mae bo. The external testimony is thus fairly evenly divided, with few but signficant representatives of the Alexandrian and Western textual clusters supporting the shorter reading. Internally, the words look like a standard scribal emendation, and may have been motivated by other healing passages where Jesus gave a similar double command (cf. Matt 9:5; Mark 2:9, [11]; Luke 5:23; [6:8]; John 5:8). On the other hand, there is some motivation for deleting ἔγειρε καί here, namely, unlike Jesus’ healing miracles, Peter raises (ἤγειρεν, ēgeiren) the man to his feet (v. 7) rather than the man rising on his own. In light of the scribal tendency to harmonize, especially in immediate context, the longer reading is slightly preferred.

verses.zh: 于是拉着他的右手，扶他起来；他的脚和踝子骨立刻健壮了，
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] Peter[NOTE:2] took hold[NOTE:3] of him by the right hand and raised him up, and at once the man’s[NOTE:4] feet and ankles were made strong.[NOTE:5]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “Then” to reflect the sequence of events.
Grk “he”; the referent (Peter) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “Peter taking hold of him…raised him up.” The participle πιάσας (piasas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Grk “his”; the referent (the man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

At once the man’s feet and ankles were made strong. Note that despite the past lameness, the man is immediately able to walk. The restoration of his ability to walk pictures the presence of a renewed walk, a fresh start at life; this was far more than money would have given him.

verses.zh: 就跳起来，站着，又行走，同他们进了殿，走着，跳着，赞美　神。
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] jumped up,[NOTE:2] stood and began walking around, and he entered the temple courts[NOTE:3] with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
notes: Grk “And he.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, the conjunction καί (kai) has not been translated here. Instead a new English sentence is begun.

Grk “Jumping up, he stood.” The participle ἐξαλλόμενος (exallomenos) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. It is possible that the paralyzed man actually jumped off the ground, but more probably this term simply refers to the speed with which he stood up. See L&N 15.240.
Grk “the temple.” This is actually a reference to the courts surrounding the temple proper, and has been translated accordingly.

verses.zh: 百姓都看见他行走，赞美　神；
verses.en: All[NOTE:1] the people saw him walking and praising God,
notes: Grk “And all.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.

verses.zh: 认得他是那素常坐在殿的美门口求周济的，就因他所遇着的事满心希奇、惊讶。
verses.en: and they recognized him as the man who used to sit and ask for donations[NOTE:1] at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and they were filled with astonishment and amazement[NOTE:2] at what had happened to him.
notes: Grk “alms,” but this term is not in common use today, so the closest modern equivalent, “donations,” is used instead. The idea is that of a donation to charity.

Amazement is a frequent response to miracles of Jesus or the apostles. These took the ancients by as much surprise as they would people today. But in terms of response to what God is doing, amazement does not equal faith (Luke 4:36; 5:9, 26; 7:16).

verses.zh: 那人正在称为所罗门的廊下，拉着彼得、约翰；众百姓一齐跑到他们那里，很觉希奇。
verses.en: While the man[NOTE:1] was hanging on to Peter and John, all the people, completely astounded, ran together to them in the covered walkway[NOTE:2] called Solomon’s Portico.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (the man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Or “portico,” “colonnade”; Grk “stoa.” The translation “covered walkway” (a descriptive translation) was used here because the architectural term “portico” or “colonnade” is less familiar. However, the more technical term “portico” was retained in the actual name that follows.

Solomon’s Portico was a covered walkway formed by rows of columns supporting a roof and open on the inner side facing the center of the temple complex. It was located on the east side of the temple (Josephus, Ant. 15.11.3-5 [15.391-420], 20.9.7 [20.221]) and was a place of commerce and conversation.

verses.zh: 彼得看见，就对百姓说：「以色列人哪，为甚么把这事当作希奇呢？为甚么定睛看我们，以为我们凭自己的能力和虔诚使这人行走呢？
verses.en: When Peter saw this, he declared to the people, “Men of Israel,[NOTE:1] why are you amazed at this? Why[NOTE:2] do you stare at us as if we had made this man[NOTE:3] walk by our own power or piety?
notes: Or perhaps “People of Israel,” since this was taking place in Solomon’s Portico and women may have been present. The Greek ἄνδρες ᾿Ισραηλῖται (andres Israēlitai) used in the plural would normally mean “men, gentlemen” (BDAG 79 s.v. ἀνήρ 1.a).
Grk “or why.”
Grk “him”; the referent (the man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 亚伯拉罕、以撒、雅各的　神，就是我们列祖的　神，已经荣耀了他的仆人（或译：儿子）耶稣；你们却把他交付彼拉多。彼拉多定意要释放他，你们竟在彼拉多面前弃绝了他。
verses.en: The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,[NOTE:1] the God of our forefathers,[NOTE:2] has glorified[NOTE:3] his servant[NOTE:4] Jesus, whom you handed over and rejected[NOTE:5] in the presence of Pilate after he had decided[NOTE:6] to release him.
notes: ‡ The repetition of ὁ θεός (ho theos, “God”) before the names of Isaac and Jacob is found in P74 א C (A D without article) 36 104 1175 lat. The omission of the second and third ὁ θεός is supported by B E Ψ 33 1739 M. The other time that Exod 3:6 is quoted in Acts (7:32) the best witnesses also lack the repeated ὁ θεός, but the three other times this OT passage is quoted in the NT the full form, with the thrice-mentioned θεός, is used (Matt 22:32; Mark 12:26; Luke 20:37). Scribes would be prone to conform the wording here to the LXX; the longer reading is thus most likely not authentic. NA28 has the words in brackets, indicating doubts as to their authenticity.

Or “ancestors”; Grk “fathers.”sn The reference to the God of the patriarchs is a reminder that God is the God of the nation and of promises. The phrase God of our forefathers is from the Hebrew scriptures (Exod 3:6, 15-16; 4:5; see also the Jewish prayer known as “The Eighteen Benedictions”). Once again, event has led to explanation, or what is called the “sign and speech” pattern.
Has glorified. Jesus is alive, raised and active, as the healing illustrates so dramatically how God honors him.
His servant. The term servant has messianic connotations given the context of the promise, the note of suffering, and the titles and functions noted in vv. 14-15.
Or “denied,” “disowned.”
This genitive absolute construction could be understood as temporal (“when he had decided”) or concessive (“although he had decided”).

verses.zh: 你们弃绝了那圣洁公义者，反求着释放一个凶手给你们。
verses.en: But you rejected[NOTE:1] the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a man who was a murderer be released to you.
notes: Or “denied,” “disowned.”

verses.zh: 你们杀了那生命的主，　神却叫他从死里复活了；我们都是为这事作见证。
verses.en: You killed[NOTE:1] the Originator[NOTE:2] of life, whom God raised[NOTE:3] from the dead. To this fact we are witnesses![NOTE:4]
notes: Or “You put to death.”
Or “Founder,” “founding Leader.”
Whom God raised. God is the main actor here, as he testifies to Jesus and vindicates him.

We are witnesses. Note the two witnesses here, Peter and John (Acts 5:32; Heb 2:3-4).tn Grk “whom God raised from the dead, of which we are witnesses.” The two consecutive relative clauses make for awkward English style, so the second was begun as a new sentence with the words “to this fact” supplied in place of the Greek relative pronoun to make a complete sentence in English.

verses.zh: 我们因信他的名，他的名便叫你们所看见所认识的这人健壮了；正是他所赐的信心，叫这人在你们众人面前全然好了。
verses.en: And on the basis of faith in Jesus’[NOTE:1] name,[NOTE:2] his very name has made this man—whom you see and know—strong. The[NOTE:3] faith that is through Jesus[NOTE:4] has given him this complete health in the presence[NOTE:5] of you all.
notes: Grk “in his name”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Here is another example of appeal to the person by mentioning the name. See the note on the word name in 3:6.
Grk “see and know, and the faith.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation and καί (kai, “and”) has not been translated.

The faith that is through Jesus. Note how this verse explains how the claim to “faith in Jesus’ name” works and what it means. To appeal to the name is to point to the person. It is not clear that the man expressed faith before the miracle. This could well be a “grace-faith miracle” where God grants power through the apostles to picture how much a gift life is (Luke 17:11-19). Christology and grace are emphasized here.tn Grk “him”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “in full view.”

verses.zh: 弟兄们，我晓得你们做这事是出于不知，你们的官长也是如此。
verses.en: And now, brothers, I know you acted in ignorance,[NOTE:1] as your rulers did too.
notes: The ignorance Peter mentions here does not excuse them from culpability. It was simply a way to say “you did not realize the great mistake you made.”

verses.zh: 但神曾藉众先知的口，预言基督将要受害，就这样应验了。
verses.en: But the things God foretold[NOTE:1] long ago through[NOTE:2] all the prophets—that his Christ[NOTE:3] would suffer—he has fulfilled in this way.
notes: God foretold. Peter’s topic is the working out of God’s plan and promise through events the scriptures also note.
Grk “by the mouth of” (an idiom).
Or “Messiah”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”sn See the note on Christ in 2:31.

verses.zh: 所以，你们当悔改归正，使你们的罪得以涂抹，
verses.en: Therefore repent and turn back so that your sins may be wiped out,

verses.zh: 这样，那安舒的日子就必从主面前来到；主也必差遣所预定给你们的基督（耶稣）降临。
verses.en: so that times of refreshing[NOTE:1] may come from the presence of the Lord,[NOTE:2] and so that he may send the Messiah[NOTE:3] appointed[NOTE:4] for you—that is, Jesus.
notes: Or “relief.”sn Times of refreshing. The phrase implies relief from difficult, distressful or burdensome circumstances. It is generally regarded as a reference to the messianic age being ushered in.

The words “so that…Lord” are traditionally placed in v. 19 by most English translations, but in the present translation the verse division follows the standard critical editions of the Greek text (NA28, UBS5).

He may send the Messiah appointed for you—that is, Jesus. The language points to the expectation of Jesus’ return to gather his people. It is a development of the question raised in Acts 1:6.tn Or “the Christ”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”
Or “designated in advance.”

verses.zh: 天必留他，等到万物复兴的时候，就是　神从创世以来、藉着圣先知的口所说的。
verses.en: This one[NOTE:1] heaven must[NOTE:2] receive until the time all things are restored,[NOTE:3] which God declared[NOTE:4] from times long ago[NOTE:5] through his holy prophets.
notes: Grk “whom,” continuing the sentence from v. 20.
The term must used here (δεῖ, dei, “it is necessary”) is a key Lukan term to point to the plan of God and what must occur.

The time all things are restored. What that restoration involves is already recorded in the scriptures of the nation of Israel.tn Grk “until the times of the restoration of all things.” Because of the awkward English style of the extended genitive construction, and because the following relative clause has as its referent the “time of restoration” rather than “all things,” the phrase was translated “until the time all things are restored.”
Or “spoke.”
Or “from all ages past.”sn From times long ago. Once again, God’s plan is emphasized.

verses.zh: 摩西曾说：『主―　神要从你们弟兄中间给你们兴起一位先知像我，凡他向你们所说的，你们都要听从。
verses.en: Moses said, ‘The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must obey[NOTE:1] him in everything he tells you.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “hear,” but the idea of “hear and obey” or simply “obey” is frequently contained in the Greek verb ἀκούω (akouō; see L&N 36.14) and the following context (v. 23) makes it clear that failure to “obey” the words of this “prophet like Moses” will result in complete destruction.
A quotation from Deut 18:15. By quoting Deut 18:15 Peter declared that Jesus was the eschatological “prophet like [Moses]” mentioned in that passage, who reveals the plan of God and the way of God.

verses.zh: 凡不听从那先知的，必要从民中全然灭绝。』
verses.en: Every person[NOTE:1] who does not obey that prophet will be destroyed and thus removed[NOTE:2] from the people.’[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “every soul” (here “soul” is an idiom for the whole person).
Or “will be completely destroyed.” In Acts 3:23 the verb ἐξολεθρεύω (exolethreuō) is translated “destroy and remove” by L&N 20.35.
A quotation from Deut 18:19, also Lev 23:29. The OT context of Lev 23:29 discusses what happened when one failed to honor atonement. One ignored the required sacrifice of God at one’s peril.

verses.zh: 从撒母耳以来的众先知，凡说预言的，也都说到这些日子。
verses.en: And all the prophets, from Samuel and those who followed him, have spoken about and announced[NOTE:1] these days.
notes: Or “proclaimed.”sn All the prophets…have spoken about and announced. What Peter preaches is rooted in basic biblical and Jewish hope as expressed in the OT scriptures.

verses.zh: 你们是先知的子孙，也承受　神与你们祖宗所立的约，就是对亚伯拉罕说：『地上万族都要因你的后裔得福。』
verses.en: You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your ancestors,[NOTE:1] saying to Abraham, ‘And in your descendants[NOTE:2] all the nations[NOTE:3] of the earth will be blessed.’[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “forefathers”; Grk “fathers.”

Or “in your offspring”; Grk “in your seed.”sn In your descendants (Grk “in your seed”). Seed has an important ambiguity in this verse. The blessing comes from the servant (v. 26), who in turn blesses the responsive children of the covenant as the scripture promised. Jesus is the seed who blesses the seed.

Or “families.” The Greek word πατριά (patria) can indicate persons of succeeding generations who are related by birth (“lineage,” “family”) but it can also indicate a relatively large unit of people who make up a sociopolitical group and who share a presumed biological descent. In many contexts πατριά is very similar to ἔθνος (ethnos) and λαός (laos). In light of the context of the OT quotation, it is better to translate πατριά as “nations” here.
A quotation from Gen 22:18.

verses.zh: 神既兴起他的仆人（或译：儿子），就先差他到你们这里来，赐福给你们，叫你们各人回转，离开罪恶。」
verses.en: God raised up[NOTE:1] his servant and sent him first to you, to bless you by turning[NOTE:2] each one of you from your iniquities.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “God raising up his servant, sent him.” The participle ἀναστήσας (anastēsas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. Some translations (e.g., NIV, NRSV) render this participle as temporal (“when God raised up his servant”).

The picture of turning is again seen as the appropriate response to the message. See v. 19 above. In v. 19 it was “turning to,” here it is “turning away from.” The direction of the two metaphors is important.

For the translation of plural πονηρία (ponēria) as “iniquities,” see G. Harder, TDNT 6:565. The plural is important, since for Luke turning to Jesus means turning away from sins, not just the sin of rejecting Jesus.
